bank.question: While preparing a patient for an orthopaedic procedure, you notice the surgical site mark is on the wrong leg according to the surgical list, though the patient is insistent the list is wrong. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: Patient safety is the priority; the procedure should be paused and the error corrected through the formal 'Time Out' or 'Sign In' protocols.
options: Proceed with the surgery as the mark is on the correct side regardless of the wrong ink colour.
Immediately call for a 'Time Out' to re-verify the site with the patient's records and consent form.
Ask the surgical scrub nurse to quickly rub out the mark and re-draw it without telling the consultant.
Wait until the patient is anaesthetised to check the records again to avoid causing the patient anxiety.

bank.question: You are an FY1 with several tasks. Which of the following should be your immediate clinical priority?
bank.explanation: Patient safety and clinical urgency take precedence over administrative handovers or minor reviews.
options: Ensure the discharge summary for a patient going home in two hours is completed.
Assess a patient who has become acutely hypotensive and tachycardic.
Document the morning ward round notes in the electronic patient record.
Review the blood results for a stable patient to see if their iron levels have improved.

bank.question: A senior colleague appears to be smelling of alcohol and is about to perform a procedure. Is it appropriate to intervene and stop them immediately?
bank.explanation: Patient safety is the top priority; if a colleague is compromised, they must be stopped immediately before they can cause harm.

bank.question: You are asked to perform an ascitic tap, a procedure you have observed once but never performed yourself. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: Working beyond your competence is a patient safety risk; you must seek supervised help to ensure the procedure is done correctly.
options: Review a YouTube video on the procedure and then attempt it alone.
Attempt the procedure anyway, as it is a common task for an FY1.
Ask the patient to wait until the morning when more staff are available.
Contact the on-call registrar to ask for supervision while you perform the procedure.

bank.question: You are starting a night shift and notice your colleague, another Foundation Doctor, smells strongly of alcohol and is slurring their words. What should you do?
bank.explanation: Professionalism and patient safety require addressing potential impairment directly and escalating to a senior if a colleague is unfit for work.
options: Ignore it as they are a senior colleague and you might be mistaken about the smell.
Offer them a strong coffee and suggest they take a quick nap in the mess.
Discreetly pull them aside to voice your concerns and, if confirmed, escalate to a senior consultant immediately.
Report them to the General Medical Council (GMC) immediately without speaking to them first.

bank.question: You observe a registrar about to administer an intravenous medication at a dose that you know is ten times the recommended amount. What do you do?
bank.explanation: Patient safety issues must be addressed immediately and directly with the individual involved to prevent harm.
options: Ignore it as they are more experienced than you.
Wait until the end of the shift to mention it privately to the registrar.
Intervene immediately and politely suggest checking the dosage against the guidelines.
Report the registrar to the General Medical Council (GMC) immediately.

bank.question: If a patient has passed away, their right to medical confidentiality no longer applies, and you can share their records with anyone who asks.
bank.explanation: Confidentiality must be maintained even after a patient's death unless there is a legal requirement or public interest to disclose.

bank.question: Your ward is severely understaffed due to sickness, and you feel the workload is becoming unsafe. What is the most appropriate first step?
bank.explanation: It is your professional duty to escalate concerns regarding understaffing that may compromise patient safety.
options: Inform the consultant on-call or the site manager about the staffing levels.
Carry as many bleeps as possible and try to finish all the work yourself.
Tell the nurses to stop calling you unless there is a cardiac arrest.
Leave the ward at your scheduled finish time regardless of the outstanding work.

bank.question: You are currently completing a complex discharge summary for a patient going to a nursing home. A nurse informs you that another patient on the ward has suddenly become very breathless. What is the best course of action?
bank.explanation: Immediate life-threatening issues (A-E assessment) take precedence over administrative tasks, even if they are urgent for other patients.
options: Apologise to the nurse and assess the breathless patient immediately using an ABCDE approach.
Finish the discharge summary first to ensure the other patient can leave the hospital on time.
Ask the nurse to take a set of observations and tell them you will be there in 30 minutes.
Call the Registrar and ask them to see the breathless patient while you finish your paperwork.

bank.question: You realise you have accidentally taken blood from the wrong patient. The samples have not yet been sent to the lab. What is your next step?
bank.explanation: Honesty and transparency (Duty of Candour) are essential; you must inform the patient and take steps to rectify the error.
options: Do nothing, as no harm was caused to the patient.
Apologise to the patient, explain the error, and arrange for the correct bloods to be taken.
Ask a nurse to retake the bloods without telling the patient why.
Cross out the old labels and write the correct details on the existing tubes.

bank.question: You have made a minor prescribing error that was caught by the pharmacist before reaching the patient. Should you still inform the patient and apologise?
bank.explanation: Openness and honesty (the Duty of Candour) are essential for maintaining trust and improving safety when errors occur.

bank.question: You overhear two colleagues discussing a patient's sensitive HIV diagnosis in a crowded hospital lift. What should you do?
bank.explanation: Respecting patient confidentiality is paramount; medical information should not be shared in public areas regardless of whether names are used.
options: Join in the conversation as it is a good learning opportunity.
Ask them for more details about the patient's history.
Politely remind your colleagues that they are in a public lift and should not discuss patients there.
Report them to the hospital's disciplinary board immediately without speaking to them.

bank.question: It is the end of your shift and you still have five non-urgent tasks outstanding due to an exceptionally busy day. What is the most professional way to handle this?
bank.explanation: Effective handover involves acknowledging and mitigating the risks of a heavy workload while ensuring the incoming team is fully informed.
options: Stay for an extra three hours to finish all the tasks yourself.
Leave the list on the computer for the next team to find without a verbal briefing.
Tell the nurses it is not your problem anymore as your shift has ended.
Perform a structured handover to the incoming team, highlighting the most urgent outstanding tasks and why they weren't finished.

bank.question: You are stuck in unexpected traffic and will be 30 minutes late for your shift. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: Professionalism includes punctuality and communication; if you are going to be late, you must inform your team so they can cover your duties.
options: Call the ward or your senior as soon as possible to let them know you are delayed.
Try to run to the ward to minimize the delay, but do not call anyone.
Wait until you arrive to explain the situation to your consultant.
Ask a friend to sign you in on the attendance sheet so it looks like you arrived on time.

bank.question: When a senior consultant regularly shouts at junior staff in front of patients, it is best to ignore it to maintain a good working relationship.
bank.explanation: Workplace bullying should be addressed through formal channels rather than being ignored, as it affects team morale and patient safety.

bank.question: A consultant repeatedly belittles your clinical decisions in front of the multidisciplinary team, making you feel undermined. What is the most appropriate step?
bank.explanation: Treating colleagues with respect is a core professional requirement; bullying or harassment should be addressed through proper workplace channels.
options: Shout back at the consultant to defend yourself.
Ignore the behaviour and hope it improves over time.
Discuss the consultant's behaviour with your educational supervisor or a trusted senior.
Post about the consultant's behaviour on a social media forum for doctors.

bank.question: You realise you have accidentally prescribed a ten-fold overdose of a medication. The patient has already received the dose but currently seems well. What should you do?
bank.explanation: Openness and honesty (Duty of Candour) are essential when an error occurs, along with taking immediate steps to rectify the mistake.
options: Wait to see if the patient develops any side effects before mentioning it.
Inform the patient of the error, apologise, and contact the senior doctor and pharmacy to mitigate any harm.
Cross out the entry on the drug chart so there is no record of the incorrect dose.
Ask a nurse to monitor the patient but do not inform the patient as it might cause unnecessary distress.

bank.question: At the end of your shift, a patient's condition is deteriorating. You have called for a review but the doctor hasn't arrived. What do you do?
bank.explanation: Effective handover involves clear communication and ensuring the receiving clinician accepts responsibility for the task.
options: Leave a note on the computer for the night team to find.
Ask the ward clerk to tell the night doctor about the patient.
Go home, as you have already stayed 15 minutes past your shift end.
Verbally hand over the patient's details and the clinical concern to the doctor taking over.

bank.question: In the UK, you must assume a patient has the capacity to make their own decisions unless it is proven that they lack it.
bank.explanation: Under the Mental Capacity Act, patients are presumed to have capacity unless proven otherwise through a formal assessment.

bank.question: A patient is about to undergo a procedure. They have signed the consent form but now express confusion about the risks. What is your action?
bank.explanation: Informed consent requires the patient to understand the risks and benefits; if they have new questions, they must be answered before proceeding.
options: Proceed with the procedure as they have already signed the consent form.
Stop, answer their questions fully, and re-confirm their consent before continuing.
Tell the patient that the consultant has already decided this is the best treatment.
Ask the nurse to sign the consent form as a witness instead.

bank.question: You are asked to treat a patient who has been admitted with a self-inflicted injury. You personally find the patient's behaviour difficult to empathise with. How should you proceed?
bank.explanation: The primary duty of a doctor is to provide care; refusing to treat based on personal disapproval of a patient's lifestyle is a breach of GMC guidance.
options: Refuse to treat the patient and ask a colleague to take over because you disagree with their choices.
Reprimand the patient for their lifestyle choices before providing any treatment.
Treat the patient with the same level of care and respect as any other patient, regardless of their background.
Provide the minimum necessary treatment and avoid any further conversation with the patient.

bank.question: A confused patient with a suspected hip fracture is refusing an X-ray. They lack the capacity to understand the risk of not having it. What do you do?
bank.explanation: When a patient is confused, clinical decisions must be made in their 'best interests' according to the Mental Capacity Act.
options: Perform the assessment in the patient's best interests to exclude life-threatening causes.
Wait until the patient regains capacity before performing any checks.
Ask the patient's next of kin to sign a consent form for the examination.
Discharge the patient as they are refusing to cooperate with medical staff.

bank.question: While handing over to the night team, you notice a patient's vitals are dropping. It is appropriate to leave the assessment entirely to the incoming team.
bank.explanation: Clinical priority and urgency must always come before administrative convenience or finishing a shift on time.

bank.question: A patient asks you for stronger painkillers while you are in the middle of documenting an urgent review of another patient. What do you do?
bank.explanation: Effective communication involves giving a clear timeframe for non-urgent tasks while acknowledging the patient's request.
options: Stop what you are doing and prescribe the painkillers immediately.
Tell the patient that you are too busy and they will have to wait several hours.
Explain that you are currently busy with a sick patient but will prescribe the pain relief as soon as you are finished.
Tell the nurse it is not your job to prescribe painkillers and they should ask a senior.

bank.question: A senior nurse on the ward frequently makes belittling comments about your clinical skills in front of patients. How should you handle this?
bank.explanation: Directly addressing the colleague allows for a quick resolution and maintains professional working relationships before involving higher management.
options: Immediately report the nurse to the Ward Manager for being unprofessional.
Ignore the comments and try to work harder to impress the nurse.
Complain about the nurse to the other Foundation Doctors in the mess.
Speak to the nurse privately and politely explain that their comments are making you feel undermined.

bank.question: You notice a nurse preparing a 10mg dose of morphine for a patient. You check the prescription and see it should be 1mg. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: Patient safety is the priority; the error must be corrected immediately, and the nurse has a right to know why you are intervening.
options: Wait until the nurse finishes and then mention it privately.
Intervene immediately and explain that the dose is incorrect according to the drug chart.
Call the consultant to report the nurse's incompetence.
Wait for the pharmacy review the next day to see if they spot it.

bank.question: When delegating a task to a medical student, you remain responsible for ensuring the task is completed safely and competently.
bank.explanation: Appropriate delegation requires ensuring the individual has the necessary skills and providing oversight as needed.

bank.question: You are an FY1. You notice a senior registrar consistently failing to wash their hands between patients and ignoring local antibiotic guidelines. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: Concerns regarding patient safety and professional standards must be escalated through the proper clinical channels immediately.
options: Escalate your concerns to the consultant or the clinical lead for the department.
Post a warning on the hospital's internal social media forum.
Ignore it as he is a senior and likely knows more than you.
Wait until your next formal appraisal to mention it to your supervisor.

bank.question: An unconscious patient is brought into A&E requiring life-saving surgery. There is no next of kin available. What is the legal basis for proceeding with treatment?
bank.explanation: In an emergency where the patient lacks capacity and no representative is available, doctors must act in the patient's best interests to save life.
options: Document that the surgery is in the patient's best interests and proceed with the emergency operation.
Wait for a court order to give permission to operate on an incapacitated patient.
Do not operate until you can find a distant relative to sign the consent form.
Perform the surgery only if the hospital chaplain agrees it is the right thing to do.

bank.question: You realise you have documented a clinical note in the wrong patient's paper handheld records. What is the most appropriate way to rectify this?
bank.explanation: Professionalism requires you to apologise and correct the mistake, ensuring the patient's record is accurate and safe.
options: Delete the entry and pretend it never happened.
Ask a colleague to cross it out so it doesn't look like your mistake.
Draw a single line through the error, sign and date it, and write the correct entry.
Use correction fluid to hide the error and write over it.

bank.question: It is professionally acceptable to start a romantic relationship with a current patient as long as you have their informed consent.
bank.explanation: The GMC requires doctors to maintain professional boundaries; personal or sexual relationships with current patients are prohibited.

bank.question: While taking blood, you accidentally use a needle that had already touched the patient's skin but was not yet used. You realize this is a minor clean technique breach. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: The GMC requires doctors to be honest and open with patients when things go wrong, known as the Duty of Candour.
options: Don't mention it unless the patient asks why their arm is bruised.
Wait for the consultant to decide if the patient needs to be told.
Inform the nursing staff but do not tell the patient to avoid causing anxiety.
Apologise to the patient, explain what happened, and monitor the site.

bank.question: You are on a public train and overhear two other doctors from your hospital discussing a patient's HIV status by name. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: Maintaining confidentiality is a core duty; patient details should never be discussed in public areas where they can be overheard.
options: Join the conversation as it is a good way to learn about interesting cases.
Politely remind your colleagues that they are in a public area and should not be discussing patient details.
Take a photo of them and report them to the hospital's Information Governance lead.
Move to a different carriage so you don't have to hear the confidential information.

bank.question: An old medical school friend who is not a patient at your hospital asks you to write a private prescription for antibiotics for her suspected UTI. What is the most appropriate response?
bank.explanation: Doctors must not provide medical treatment to those with whom they have a close personal relationship if other options are available.
options: Write the prescription as it is an emergency and saves her a GP visit.
Politely decline and advise her to see her own GP or attend an Urgent Care Centre.
Ask a colleague to write the prescription using your name to avoid a conflict of interest.
Perform a full clinical examination in the hospital and then write the prescription.

bank.question: Posting a redacted photo of an interesting X-ray on a public social media account without explicit patient consent is a breach of professional standards.
bank.explanation: Social media activity should not undermine public trust in the profession or identify patients, even in 'private' groups.

bank.question: You are finishing some urgent discharge summaries (TTOs) when a nurse tells you a patient has a new blood pressure reading of 85/50. What is your immediate priority?
bank.explanation: Patient safety is the absolute priority; a patient who is acutely unwell and potentially unstable must be seen before routine administrative tasks.
options: Assess the patient with the low blood pressure immediately.
Finish the TTOs so the other patients can be discharged on time.
Call the registrar and ask them to see the unwell patient while you finish the TTOs.
Ask the nurse to take another set of obs in an hour to see if the pressure improves.

bank.question: Your registrar asks you to perform a lumbar puncture. You have never done one before and do not feel confident. What is your best response?
bank.explanation: When faced with an unfamiliar task, it is safest to admit limitations and seek supervision rather than risking patient safety.
options: Attempt the procedure anyway, as you saw it done once in medical school.
Look up a video on your phone and then perform the procedure on the patient.
Explain to your senior that you don't feel competent to do it alone and ask if they can supervise you.
Ask the patient if they mind if you 'practice' the procedure on them for the first time.

bank.question: You made a minor prescribing error that was caught by the pharmacist before the patient took the medication. No harm was caused. What is the best way to handle this for your professional development?
bank.explanation: Reflecting on mistakes is a key part of medical practice and professional development.
options: Try to forget about it to maintain your confidence.
Keep it to yourself to avoid looking incompetent to your supervisors.
Discuss the incident with your educational supervisor and record a reflection in your portfolio.
Wait for the patient to complain before taking any action.

bank.question: If a patient is deemed to lack capacity for one specific medical decision, they are automatically deemed to lack capacity for all medical decisions.
bank.explanation: Capacity is 'decision-specific'; a patient may have the capacity to choose their meal but not to consent to a complex surgery.

bank.question: A 75-year-old patient with full capacity refuses a life-saving blood transfusion due to their personal beliefs. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: You must respect a patient's autonomy and right to refuse treatment, even if that refusal may result in death, provided they have capacity.
options: Give the treatment anyway as it is in their best interest to stay alive.
Respect the patient's wish and document their refusal and your assessment of their capacity.
Tell the patient they are being irrational and must take the medicine.
Ask the patient's next of kin to sign a consent form on their behalf.

bank.question: You notice a medical student on your team crying in the staff room after a difficult conversation with a consultant. What should you do?
bank.explanation: Supporting colleagues and maintaining team morale is important, provided it does not compromise clinical duties.
options: Tell them to stop crying and get back to work because the ward is busy.
Report them to the Deanery for being emotionally unstable.
Ignore them to give them privacy and hope they feel better later.
Ask a colleague to cover your bleep for 10 minutes so you can take the student to a quiet room and support them.

bank.question: You are called to see a patient who is becoming increasingly short of breath and tachycardic. You are unsure of the cause. What is the most appropriate next step?
bank.explanation: As an FY1, you must recognise the limits of your competence and seek senior help for a patient who is significantly deteriorating.
options: Increase the oxygen and check back in two hours.
Ask the ward sister what she thinks you should do.
Prescribe a new antibiotic and wait for the morning ward round.
Perform an ABCDE assessment and call your registrar for urgent review.

bank.question: If chronic understaffing is putting patient safety at risk, doctors have a professional obligation to raise these concerns with their management.
bank.explanation: Medical professionals have a duty to speak up about systemic issues that may compromise the standard of care provided to patients.

bank.question: A registrar makes a derogatory comment about your medical school in front of a patient. You feel embarrassed and undermined. What should you do?
bank.explanation: Bullying and harassment are unacceptable; addressing the behaviour directly and professionally is the first step in conflict resolution.
options: Speak to the registrar privately and explain how their comments made you feel.
Ignore the registrar and try to avoid working with them in the future.
Immediately file a formal grievance with the British Medical Association (BMA).
Tell the registrar's consultant that the registrar is a bully.

bank.question: A medical student asks if they can join you while you examine a patient with a rare heart murmur. How should you respond?
bank.explanation: Teaching and training lower-level staff is a professional responsibility, but should be balanced with time management and clinical priority.
options: Invite the student to observe the examination and explain your findings and reasoning as you go.
Tell the student you are too busy and they should go to the library to read instead.
Ask the student to perform the entire examination and then leave without checking their work.
Ask the student to wait in the corridor while you see the patient and then give them a 30-second summary later.

bank.question: An unconscious patient arrives in A&E needing emergency surgery to stop internal bleeding. There is no family present. What is the most appropriate legal basis for proceeding?
bank.explanation: In an emergency where a patient lacks capacity and no legal representative is available, doctors must act in the patient's best interests.
options: Wait for the hospital's legal team to provide advice.
Wait for the next of kin to arrive to get their permission.
Proceed with the surgery as it is a life-saving necessity in the patient's best interests.
Do not operate until the patient regains consciousness to provide consent.

bank.question: A doctor can refuse to treat a patient based on the doctor's personal disapproval of the patient's lifestyle or religious beliefs.
bank.explanation: Doctors may only decline to perform a procedure based on conscientious objection (e.g., abortion) if it does not result in the patient being denied access to care.

bank.question: A patient you are treating on the ward discovers you both enjoy the same hobby and invites you to join their local club meeting next week. What is the most appropriate response?
bank.explanation: Maintaining professional boundaries is essential; doctors must not use their position to pursue personal or sexual relationships with patients.
options: Accept the invite as it would be rude to refuse a kind gesture.
Politely decline the invite, explaining that it is not professional for you to meet socially.
Accept the invite but only if you can bring a colleague along.
Wait until the patient is discharged and then accept the invitation.

bank.question: During a ward round, you hear a fellow Foundation Doctor give a patient incorrect information regarding the risks of a procedure. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: Patient safety and immediate feedback are the priorities. Speaking to the colleague directly allows them to correct the error and learn from it.
options: Wait until the ward round is over and then report the colleague to their consultant.
Pull the colleague aside at the next available opportunity and explain why their advice was incorrect.
Interrupt the colleague in front of the patient to ensure the patient receives the correct information immediately.
Say nothing to the colleague, but go back to the patient later and give them the correct advice.

bank.question: You realise you have accidentally applied the wrong patient's ID stickers to a set of blood tubes you just collected. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: Patient safety is the priority; the error must be corrected immediately by relabelling and informing the team, followed by formal notification.
options: Wait until the shift ends to let the ward clerk know.
Discard the samples and pretend the blood draw failed.
Inform the nurse in charge and the laboratory immediately so the records can be corrected.
Ask a colleague to re-bleed the patient so you don't get in trouble.

bank.question: If a patient is harmed during their care, the medical team has a legal and professional 'Duty of Candour' to inform them and offer an apology.
bank.explanation: Openness and honesty are essential when things go wrong; the professional duty of candour applies even if the patient has not yet complained.

bank.question: A patient you recently treated sends you a friend request on a personal social media platform. How should you respond?
bank.explanation: Maintaining professional boundaries is essential; social media contact with current patients is generally inappropriate and should be politely declined.
options: Politely decline the request, explaining that you maintain professional boundaries with patients.
Accept the request but never interact with their posts.
Block the patient immediately without saying anything to them.
Accept the request and message them to ask how their recovery is going.

bank.question: You prescribed a dose of analgesia for a patient in pain an hour ago, but notice it has not been administered. The nurse responsible appears busy. What should you do?
bank.explanation: It is important to understand the nurse's perspective and rationale before taking further action, as there may be clinical reasons for the delay.
options: Immediately report the nurse to the Ward Manager for failing to follow your instructions.
Administer the medication yourself to ensure the patient receives it on time.
Inform the patient that their medication is late because the nurse has not given it yet.
Speak to the nurse privately to ask why the medication has not been administered as prescribed.

bank.question: You are working with a registrar and notice they smell strongly of alcohol and are slurring their words during a ward round. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: Patient safety comes first. Any suspected impairment of a colleague must be escalated immediately to a senior who can take action.
options: Ignore it as you might be mistaken about the smell.
Wait until the end of the shift and ask the registrar if they have been drinking.
Discreetly inform your consultant or the on-call lead immediately.
Tell the registrar to go home and cover their patients for them.

bank.question: It is acceptable to discuss the clinical details of a specific patient in a private Facebook group for doctors, provided the patient is not named.
bank.explanation: Patient confidentiality must be maintained on social media even in private groups, as information can still be leaked or traced back to the patient.

bank.question: A patient with advanced dementia and a suspected pneumonia is refusing a necessary cannulation. They lack capacity to understand the consequences. What is the correct legal approach?
bank.explanation: When a patient lacks capacity, doctors must act in their 'best interests' while still trying to involve them and their family in the decision.
options: Wait for the patient's next of kin to arrive before giving any treatment.
Perform the procedure in the patient's best interests as it is clinically necessary and urgent.
Discharge the patient as they are refusing treatment.
Apply for a court order to perform the procedure.

bank.question: A patient with a serious infection refuses to take their prescribed intravenous antibiotics, stating they 'don't like needles.' How should you first approach this?
bank.explanation: Building a rapport and understanding the patient's concerns is the first step in addressing non-compliance and ensuring they understand the risks.
options: Sit down with the patient and ask them to explain their reasons for refusing the medication.
Tell the patient they will not be allowed to go home unless they take the prescribed treatment.
Ask a senior doctor to speak to the patient and tell them they must take the medicine.
Document the refusal in the notes and move on to the next patient to avoid wasting time.

bank.question: You accidentally prescribed the wrong dose of a medication. The nurse caught the error before administration. What is your next step regarding the patient?
bank.explanation: The Duty of Candour requires being open and honest with patients when something goes wrong, regardless of whether harm occurred.
options: Nothing, as no harm was caused to the patient.
Tell the pharmacist to keep it quiet so you don't lose your license.
Only document it in the patient's notes but don't tell the patient.
Apologise to the patient, explain what happened, and document the error.

bank.question: A doctor can legally provide contraceptive advice to a minor under 16 without parental consent if the minor is deemed 'Gillick competent'.
bank.explanation: The Fraser Guidelines (and Gillick competence) allow clinicians to provide contraceptive advice or treatment to under-16s without parental consent in specific circumstances.

bank.question: An unidentified, unconscious patient is brought to A&E with a tension pneumothorax. No family is present. What should you do?
bank.explanation: In an emergency, life-saving treatment should not be delayed by paperwork if the patient is in immediate danger.
options: Wait for the patient to regain consciousness to get consent.
Call the hospital legal team for advice before acting.
Proceed with the emergency treatment to save the patient's life.
Try to find a friend or relative to sign the consent form on their behalf.

bank.question: Your shift ended 30 minutes ago. You still have two non-urgent discharge summaries to write and one set of routine bloods to review. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: Doctors must prioritize tasks based on clinical urgency. Handing over stable tasks allows for proper rest and safe patient care.
options: Stay until all tasks are completed, regardless of how long it takes.
Complete the bloods but leave the discharge summaries for the day team without telling them.
Hand over the outstanding tasks to the incoming night team, prioritising the urgent blood results.
Ask the ward nurse to do the blood tests while you finish the discharge summaries.

bank.question: A senior nurse shouts at you in front of a patient because you haven't finished a discharge summary. You feel humiliated. What is the best way to handle this?
bank.explanation: Acknowledge the stress of the environment but maintain professional standards and address the behaviour calmly in private.
options: Speak to the nurse privately later to explain how their tone was unprofessional.
Shout back at the nurse so they know you won't be bullied.
Report the nurse to the Nursing and Midwifery Council immediately.
Ignore it and hope it doesn't happen again.

bank.question: If a junior doctor is feeling severely unwell but the ward is short-staffed, they should continue working until the shift ends to support their team.
bank.explanation: Working while unwell can compromise patient safety; it is the doctor's responsibility to recognize when their own health affects their judgment.

bank.question: You notice a fellow FY1 has been increasingly withdrawn, making minor clinical errors, and arriving late to shifts. What should you do?
bank.explanation: Concerns about a colleague's performance or health should be raised with a supervisor to ensure patient safety and colleague support.
options: Assume they are just tired and do nothing.
Privately ask your colleague if they are okay and mention your observations to your supervisor.
Tell the other FY1s that you think this colleague is incompetent.
Check the colleague's medical records to see if they have a health condition.

bank.question: You are examining a 4-year-old child and notice several bruises in different stages of healing. The mother asks you not to tell anyone. What is your primary responsibility?
bank.explanation: While confidentiality is vital, the immediate safety of the child is the priority. Concerns of abuse must be escalated to the designated safeguarding lead.
options: Respect the mother's request for confidentiality to maintain the doctor-patient relationship.
Follow the local trust's safeguarding policy and discuss your concerns with the safeguarding lead.
Wait until the child is seen again in a week to see if more bruises appear before taking action.
Call the police immediately to have the mother arrested for suspected child abuse.

bank.question: You are asked to cannulate an easy-to-bleed patient for fluids. You have done this many times, but you are feeling tired. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: While you should seek help for complex tasks, you are expected to take initiative for basic clinical tasks you have been trained for.
options: Refuse to do it because you are too busy.
Wait for the consultant to show you how to do it.
Ask the patient to wait until the morning.
Attempt the cannulation yourself as it is a basic skill you are competent in.

bank.question: Written consent is legally required before a doctor can perform a routine venepuncture (blood draw) on an adult with full capacity.
bank.explanation: Verbal consent is often sufficient for minor, non-invasive procedures like blood tests, provided the patient understands the process.

bank.question: A patient on the operating table, just before anaesthesia, says they are no longer sure they want the surgery. What is the correct action?
bank.explanation: Consent is a continuous process; if a patient expresses new doubts, the procedure must stop until their concerns are addressed.
options: Continue with the procedure as they already signed the form.
Tell them it's too late to change their mind.
Stop the procedure immediately and re-explain the risks and benefits.
Sedate the patient so they are less anxious and continue.

bank.question: A senior staff nurse frequently ignores your clinical requests and speaks to you dismissively in front of the multidisciplinary team. How should you handle this?
bank.explanation: The first step in resolving a recurring conflict is an informal, private discussion to address the behaviour and its impact on the working environment.
options: Report the nurse to the Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) for unprofessionalism.
Ignore the comments and focus on your work to avoid further conflict.
Complain about the nurse to your Consultant at your next scheduled meeting.
Request a private meeting with the nurse to discuss how their comments make you feel.

bank.question: You are caring for a patient whose NEWS2 score has risen to 7. You have bleeped your registrar twice with no response. What is the next step?
bank.explanation: Escalation is key when a patient is deteriorating. If the registrar is unavailable, the next level of seniority must be contacted.
options: Wait another 30 minutes for the registrar to respond.
Call the consultant on-call or the outreach team immediately.
Try to manage the situation alone using Google.
Ask the patient's family what they think should be done.

bank.question: It is generally considered poor professional practice for a doctor to prescribe controlled medications for a close family member.
bank.explanation: GMC guidance states doctors should avoid treating themselves or those with whom they have a close personal relationship except in emergencies.

bank.question: You want to share an interesting clinical case on a professional doctors' forum for educational purposes. What must you ensure?
bank.explanation: Sharing clinical experiences for learning is good practice, but all identifying details must be removed to protect patient confidentiality.
options: Ensure the case is completely anonymised so the patient cannot be identified.
Include the patient's initials and ward name so colleagues know who you mean.
Ask the patient for written permission to post it on your private Facebook.
Only post it if you have 100 or fewer followers.

bank.question: You realise you forgot to document a patient review you conducted four hours ago. You are still on the ward. What is the most appropriate way to document this?
bank.explanation: Clinical documentation must be accurate and truthful. Backdating is dishonest and professional misconduct. Retrospective entries must be clearly labelled.
options: Backdate the entry to the time the patient was actually seen to ensure the notes are chronologically correct.
Don't bother writing an entry as the patient is already being discharged and it won't change management.
Make an entry now, clearly stating the current time and that it is a retrospective note of the earlier review.
Ask a colleague who was also there to write the note for you so it looks like it was done on time.

bank.question: You are an FY1. A nurse informs you that a patient who was stable has suddenly become confused and has a heart rate of 120 bpm. You are not sure what is wrong. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: Patient safety is clinical priority. If you are unsure and the patient is unwell, you must seek senior advice immediately while performing an initial assessment.
options: Ask the nurse to re-check the observations in 30 minutes to see if they improve.
Perform an immediate A-E assessment and bleep your senior for urgent review.
Request a portable chest X-ray and wait for the results before calling your senior.
Prescribe a bolus of intravenous fluids as the patient is likely dehydrated.

bank.question: A doctor may breach patient confidentiality without consent if they believe the patient poses a serious risk of physical violence to an identified person.
bank.explanation: Confidentiality is not absolute and must be breached if there is a significant risk of death or serious harm to a third party.

bank.question: A member of the hospital domestic staff approaches you in the corridor, complaining of persistent abdominal pain and asking for your medical advice. What is the most appropriate response?
bank.explanation: Providing medical advice outside of a formal clinical setting is risky and unprofessional. You should encourage them to use the appropriate NHS pathways.
options: Look up her symptoms on the hospital's computer system to provide a second opinion.
Advise her on which specific medication she should ask her GP to prescribe.
Advise her to book an appointment with her GP or contact NHS 111 for clinical advice.
Perform a quick physical examination in the staff room to reassure her.

bank.question: A ward pharmacist leaves a note stating they disagree with the antibiotic you have chosen for a patient's pneumonia. What should you do?
bank.explanation: A collaborative approach that acknowledges the pharmacist's expertise while explaining the clinical reasoning is the most professional way to resolve a disagreement.
options: Call the pharmacist to discuss their concerns and explain the clinical reasoning behind your choice.
Change the prescription immediately to what the pharmacist suggested as they are the experts.
Ignore the pharmacist's note and tell the nurses to administer the drug as you originally wrote it.
Contact your Registrar and ask them to tell the pharmacist to stop interfering with your prescriptions.

bank.question: A final-year medical student asks if they can perform a lumbar puncture on a patient. You have seen them perform it once before under supervision. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: Medical students must be supervised and patients must give informed consent for students to perform procedures. Safety and consent are paramount.
options: Explain that the student must be supervised by a competent clinician and ask the patient for their consent.
Allow the student to perform the procedure alone to build their confidence.
Tell the student they are not allowed to perform procedures on the ward under any circumstances.
Ask the student to wait until you are less busy, then let them try without mentioning it to the patient.

bank.question: If an adult patient lacks capacity, their next of kin has the legal authority to sign a consent form for a non-urgent surgical procedure.
bank.explanation: Consent must be sought from the patient or a legal proxy; relatives do not have the automatic legal right to consent on behalf of an adult lacking capacity.

bank.question: A consultant is about to break bad news to a family. They ask you, the FY1, to join them. You have a lot of administrative tasks to finish. What should you do?
bank.explanation: While you should not take the lead, staying to observe provides a learning opportunity and allows you to support the team if needed after the news is broken.
options: Insist on breaking the news yourself to gain experience for your portfolio.
Wait outside the room so the consultant and family have more privacy.
Attend the meeting to observe the consultant and offer support to the family afterwards.
Go to the ward kitchen to prepare tea for the family while the consultant talks to them.

bank.question: You receive a phone call from someone claiming to be a patient's daughter, asking for a clinical update. The patient is conscious and has capacity. What is your first step?
bank.explanation: Doctors have a duty to protect patient confidentiality. If a third party calls, you must confirm the patient's identity and their consent before sharing information.
options: Give a full update on the patient's condition to the caller immediately.
Explain that you cannot give information over the phone without confirming the patient's consent.
Tell the caller you are too busy to talk and hang up the phone.
Give vague information about the patient being 'stable' without giving specific clinical details.

bank.question: You are about to perform an arterial blood gas (ABG) on a patient. What is the most important step to take before you begin?
bank.explanation: Verifying the patient's identity via their wristband is a critical safety step to ensure the right treatment is given to the right patient.
options: Check the patient's wristband and ask them to state their full name and date of birth.
Check the name on the end of the bed and proceed with the procedure.
Ask the nurse 'Is this Mr Smith in bed 4?' before starting the procedure.
Assume the patient is who they say they are if they nod when you say a name.

bank.question: A valid 'living will' or Advanced Decision refusing specific life-sustaining treatment must be followed even if the medical team believes the treatment is in the patient's best interests.
bank.explanation: An Advanced Decision to Refuse Treatment (ADRT) is legally binding in England and Wales if it is valid and applicable to the current situation.

bank.question: A consultant asks you to change your previous entry in a patient's medical notes to reflect a different diagnosis that makes the department's statistics look better. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: This is a matter of professional integrity and patient safety. Clinical records must be accurate and never falsified, regardless of the person's seniority.
options: Change the notes as requested, as the consultant is ultimately responsible for the patient.
Refuse to change the notes but do not document the request.
Politely refuse and offer to write a new entry reflecting the current clinical plan.
Report the consultant to the General Medical Council (GMC) immediately.

bank.question: You see a fellow FY1 struggling to cannulate a patient who is becoming increasingly distressed. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: In an emergency, safety is the priority. If a colleague is struggling with a procedure, offering to help (if competent) or finding someone who can is the best course of action.
options: Take the needle out of the colleague's hand and do it yourself without saying anything.
Walk away to avoid making the colleague feel more nervous than they already are.
Ask the colleague if they would like you to take over or assist them with the procedure.
Call the Consultant immediately to report that the colleague is incompetent at cannulation.

bank.question: You receive a phone call from someone claiming to be a patient's daughter, asking for an update on her father's condition. You do not recognize the voice. What should you do?
bank.explanation: Confidentiality must be maintained. You cannot confirm or deny a patient's presence without their explicit consent, even to family members over the phone.
options: Tell the caller the patient's current condition and their expected discharge date.
Explain that you cannot disclose any information and ask the caller to contact the patient's 'next of kin'.
Transfer the call directly to the patient's bedside phone so they can talk.
Confirm the patient is on the ward but refuse to give clinical details.

bank.question: If a patient offers a doctor a high-value cash gift as a thank-you after a successful surgery, it is acceptable to accept it for personal use.
bank.explanation: Accepting significant gifts can create a conflict of interest or the perception of one; small tokens may be okay, but expensive gifts should be politely declined.

bank.question: It is 4:45 PM and you have three 'urgent' tasks remaining, but you are also being asked to sign a discharge letter. You feel overwhelmed. What is the best course of action?
bank.explanation: Teamwork and honesty are essential. Admitting when you are overwhelmed allows the team to redistribute tasks safely.
options: Stay 4 hours late to finish everything yourself without telling anyone.
Leave the remaining tasks for the night team without informing them.
Tell the nurse you are too busy and they will have to find someone else to help.
Inform your senior that you are struggling and work together to prioritise the most urgent tasks.

bank.question: You accidentally prescribed 50mg of a drug instead of 5mg. The patient took the dose but is currently asymptomatic. What should you do?
bank.explanation: Open and honest communication (Duty of Candour) is essential when an error occurs. You should inform the patient, apologize, and outline the steps for monitoring.
options: Don't say anything to the patient, as the dose was only slightly higher and unlikely to cause harm.
Wait for the senior consultant to tell the patient during the morning ward round.
Blame the pharmacy for not catching the error before the medication reached the ward.
Apologise to the patient, explain the error, and inform them of how they will be monitored for side effects.

bank.question: A grateful patient offers you a GBP 50 gift voucher for a local department store as a thank you for your care. What is the most appropriate response?
bank.explanation: Maintaining professional boundaries is required by GMC guidance. You should politely decline while acknowledging the patient's kind gesture to maintain the doctor-patient relationship.
options: Accept the gift but donate it to the ward's charity fund.
Politely decline the gift, explaining that hospital policy and professional guidance prevent you from accepting it.
Accept the gift and use it for your next holiday as a reward for your hard work.
Tell the patient that the gift is not expensive enough to be a problem and take it home.

bank.question: On a hospital ward, the Consultant is the only staff member who is legally accountable for any clinical errors made by the junior doctors on the team.
bank.explanation: While the consultant has ultimate responsibility, every member of the team is professionally accountable for their own actions and omissions.

bank.question: A patient becomes physically aggressive and starts throwing items in the ward bay. What should be your first priority?
bank.explanation: When patients are aggressive, the first priority is the safety of staff and other patients. Seeking security assistance and involving seniors is appropriate.
options: Step back, call for security assistance, and inform your senior.
Shout back at the patient to show them you are in charge of the situation.
Try to physically restrain the patient yourself to prevent them from leaving.
Ignore the patient's behaviour and continue trying to explain the treatment plan.

bank.question: You are concerned that a senior consultant's health is deteriorating, leading to several near-misses and errors in theatre. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: If a consultant's health or behaviour may be putting patients at risk, you have a professional obligation to raise these concerns through the appropriate senior channels.
options: Discuss your concerns confidentially with your Clinical Supervisor or the Head of Department.
Confront the consultant directly during a ward round about their recent poor performance.
Tell the patients that the consultant is currently unwell and they should ask for a second opinion.
Do nothing, as it is not your place as a junior doctor to question the health of a senior consultant.

bank.question: You wake up with a high fever, a cough, and a sore throat on a morning when your ward is short-staffed. What should you do?
bank.explanation: If you are unwell, you are a risk to patients and colleagues. You must follow local sickness protocols and stay home to recover.
options: Go to work anyway but wear a mask all day and avoid high-risk patients.
Go to work and ask your registrar if it is okay for you to stay.
Call your department and the rota coordinator as soon as possible to report your absence.
Wait until your shift starts, then go to A&E to be seen as a patient yourself.

bank.question: Missing a formal clinical handover to leave a shift on time is considered a breach of professional standards and a risk to patient safety.
bank.explanation: Effective handover is critical for patient safety; skipping it to leave on time increases the risk of missed information and adverse events.

bank.question: You notice a fellow FY1 has been smelling of stale tobacco, looking unkempt, and making repetitive mistakes with fluid prescriptions. What is the most appropriate initial step?
bank.explanation: If you believe a colleague's health is affecting their performance or patient safety, you have a duty to raise concerns through the correct channels.
options: Wait and see if their performance improves over the next few weeks.
Ask other colleagues if they have noticed the same issues before doing anything.
Take over all of their clinical tasks so they can rest in the staff room.
Speak to the colleague privately to express your concern and advise them to speak to their supervisor.

bank.question: A nurse informs you that a patient who was stable for discharge has developed a new fever and a cough. Is the most appropriate initial action?
bank.explanation: Patient safety and physical assessment take priority when a patient's condition changes; clinical review is essential before deciding on imaging or discharge.
options: Request an urgent chest X-ray to rule out pneumonia immediately.
Ask the nurse to give the patient paracetamol and reassess in four hours.
Perform an A-E clinical assessment of the patient immediately.
Wait for the consultant ward round to discuss the change in observations.

bank.question: You are an FY1 examining a patient with shortness of breath. You think you hear fine crackles at the lung bases, but you are not confident in your auscultation skills. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: Patient safety is paramount; if you are unsure of a clinical finding, you must seek senior verification before starting treatment.
options: Treat the patient for a heart failure exacerbation based on your findings.
Ask your senior or the ward registrar to review the patient's chest sounds.
Check the patient's previous notes and follow the last documented plan.
Order a chest X-ray and wait for the report before taking any further action.

bank.question: When making a 'best interests' decision for a patient lacking capacity, the doctor must consider if there is a way to achieve the outcome that is less restrictive of the patient's rights.
bank.explanation: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (England and Wales), decisions for those lacking capacity must be the least restrictive of their future rights and freedoms.

bank.question: You need to take blood from a patient who is currently reading a book. They do not appear distressed. What should you do first?
bank.explanation: Verbal consent is necessary even for minor procedures; it ensures the patient is informed and willing to proceed.
options: Explain the procedure and ask the patient if they are happy for you to proceed.
Proceed with the blood draw as the patient has already agreed to the admission.
Ask the patient to sign a formal written consent form before taking blood.
Tell the patient that the blood test is mandatory for their treatment.

bank.question: You are using a medical device that malfunctions during a procedure, luckily without causing harm to the patient. What is the most important next step?
bank.explanation: Clinical governance and safety require that significant errors are reported formally through systems like Datix to ensure organisational learning.
options: Inform the consultant and suggest they talk to the pharmacy about it.
Complete a formal incident report (e.g. Datix) regarding the equipment failure.
Email the equipment manufacturer directly to complain.
Advise the nursing staff to throw away all similar devices on the ward.

bank.question: A more senior colleague frequently speaks to you in a condescending tone in the staff room, making you feel undervalued. What is the most appropriate initial action?
bank.explanation: Professionalism involves addressing issues directly and calmly with colleagues to maintain a good working relationship and clarify expectations.
options: Report your colleague to the Clinical Lead for bullying and lack of professionalism.
Publicly confront your colleague the next time they speak to you in that manner.
Speak to your colleague privately to explain how their tone makes you feel and seek a resolution.
Ignore the behaviour and try to finish your tasks faster to avoid further conflict.

bank.question: If a patient is distressed, it is professionally appropriate for a doctor to share their personal religious beliefs to provide comfort, even if the patient has not asked for them.
bank.explanation: The GMC states doctors must not express personal beliefs to patients in ways that exploit their vulnerability or cause them distress.

bank.question: While in the hospital canteen, you notice a printed patient handover list lying on an empty table. What should you do?
bank.explanation: Protecting patient confidentiality involves ensuring that sensitive information is not visible to unauthorized persons in public areas.
options: Finish your dinner first, as you have had a long shift and need a break.
Look at the list to see which doctor left it there so you can return it to them later.
Ask the canteen staff to put an announcement over the loudspeaker about the lost list.
Immediately pick up the list and dispose of it in a confidential waste bin.

bank.question: A registrar asks you to perform an ascitic tap. You have seen it done once but have never performed it yourself. What is the most appropriate response?
bank.explanation: You must always work within your competency. Observing first is the safest way to learn while ensuring the patient receives skilled care.
options: Ask the registrar to perform it while you observe and assist.
Attempt the procedure after watching a video tutorial on your phone.
Ask a fellow Foundation Doctor who has done it once before to guide you.
Refuse to be involved and continue with your other ward tasks.

bank.question: You realise you have accidentally prescribed a double dose of a regular laxative. The patient has already taken it. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: Openness and honesty (Duty of Candour) are essential; you must inform the patient of errors and ensure they are not harmed.
options: Wait until the next morning to see if the patient develops any side effects.
Inform the patient of the error, apologise, and monitor them for adverse effects.
Correct the drug chart and say nothing, as the dose difference was very small.
Ask the nurse not to file an incident report since no harm was caused.

bank.question: In an emergency situation where a patient is unconscious and requires life-saving treatment, it is legally permissible to proceed without waiting for formal consent.
bank.explanation: In a clinical emergency, doctors may provide life-saving treatment even if the patient lacks capacity and cannot consent, provided it is in their best interests.

bank.question: A medical student on your team tells you they have been feeling very low and are struggling to get out of bed in the morning. What is the best response?
bank.explanation: The primary concern is the student's health and potential risk to patients. They should be encouraged to seek professional medical advice.
options: Suggest that the student takes some over-the-counter painkillers and continues the placement.
Tell the student to go home and not return until they have seen a specialist.
Advise the student to see their GP or Occupational Health and offer to help them leave the ward.
Inform the University immediately that the student is unfit to practice medicine.

bank.question: A registrar repeatedly makes jokes about your medical school's reputation in front of the nursing staff, making you feel uncomfortable. How should you handle this?
bank.explanation: Professionalism requires managing interpersonal conflicts directly and privately before involving seniors, unless the behavior persists or impacts safety.
options: Report the registrar to the Clinical Lead for bullying.
Ignore the comments and focus on your clinical work.
Make a joke about the registrar's own mistakes in front of the team.
Ask to speak to the registrar privately to discuss how their comments affect you.

bank.question: A patient's condition is deteriorating rapidly. You have tried to contact your registrar several times without success. What should you do?
bank.explanation: Escalation is vital when a patient's condition is beyond your competency; if the registrar is unavailable, go to the consultant.
options: Stay with the patient and continue to monitor their vitals every 15 minutes.
Ask the nurse to try bleeping the registrar again every 5 minutes until they answer.
Attempt a procedure you have only seen once to try and stabilise the patient.
Contact the Consultant on-call immediately to report the patient's deterioration.

bank.question: If you are invited to a departmental social lunch, it is acceptable to skip the midday clinical handover as long as the nurses are present on the ward.
bank.explanation: Handover is a critical point for patient safety; skipping it to attend an social event is a breach of professional duties.

bank.question: A nurse asks you to perform a nasogastric (NG) tube insertion. You have only ever practiced this on a mannequin. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: Acting within your level of competence is a core GMC requirement. You should never perform a procedure alone if you are not confident.
options: Attempt the procedure anyway to avoid delaying the patient's treatment.
Explain to the nurse that you are not yet competent to do this alone and ask for senior supervision.
Ask the nurse to do it instead, as they have probably seen it done many times.
Look up a video of the procedure on your phone and then try to perform it.

bank.question: A patient scheduled for an elective procedure tells you they are 'having second thoughts' and are not sure they want to go ahead. What is the best action?
bank.explanation: Consent must be informed. If a patient is hesitant, it is the doctor's duty to explore their concerns and ensure they understand the risks and benefits.
options: Ask the nurse to convince the patient while you see other people.
Note the refusal in the charts and cancel the procedure.
Sit down with the patient to explore their specific concerns and provide more information.
Tell the patient they will likely die if they do not have the procedure.

bank.question: You suspect a fellow FY1 is coming to work under the influence of alcohol, as you can smell it on their breath during morning handover. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: When patient safety is potentially compromised by a colleague's health or behaviour, you have a professional duty to report it to a senior.
options: Discreetly inform your consultant or the educational supervisor about your concerns.
Follow your colleague around the ward to ensure they do not make any major mistakes.
Organise a social event for the team to help your colleague feel more included.
Tell the nursing staff to double-check all of that colleague's prescriptions.

bank.question: A GP surgery may legally remove a patient from its list if the professional relationship has completely broken down, provided the patient is given adequate notice.
bank.explanation: While rare, the GMC allows for this if the relationship with the patient has broken down or trust has vanished, following specific formal procedures.

bank.question: You are finishing a discharge summary for a patient who is waiting to go home. A nurse calls you to see another patient who has developed sudden chest pain. What should you do?
bank.explanation: Clinical prioritisation is essential. You must deal with the most acutely unwell patient first while ensuring other tasks are covered.
options: Finish the discharge summary first so the bed can be cleared for a new admission.
Ask the nurse to wait 10 minutes while you finish your current task.
Attend to the patient with chest pain immediately and ask a colleague to help with the discharge.
Tell the patient with chest pain that you will be there as soon as you have finished your work.

bank.question: Your shift is ending, but a blood result for a patient with suspected sepsis is still pending. What is the most appropriate way to manage this?
bank.explanation: Handover is a critical safety moment. Unfinished tasks must be communicated clearly to the incoming team to ensure continuity of care.
options: Hand over the outstanding blood result to the night team to follow up.
Stay late until the result comes back, regardless of how long it takes.
Leave a note on the computer screen for the morning team.
Assume the lab will call the ward if the result is significantly abnormal.

bank.question: You realise you have written a clinical note in the wrong patient's paper medical records. What is the correct way to rectify this?
bank.explanation: Good documentation requires that any corrections are clear, timed, dated, and signed, without obscuring the original entry.
options: Draw a single line through the error, write the correction next to it, then sign and date it.
Use correction fluid to cover the error and write the correct information over the top.
Scribble out the mistake until it is unreadable so that no one is confused by it.
Ignore the mistake and write a new entry at the bottom of the page with the correct info.

bank.question: A doctor must obtain formal written consent before performing a routine, non-invasive blood pressure check on a patient who has the capacity to consent.
bank.explanation: Verbal or non-verbal consent is sufficient for routine, non-invasive observations like blood pressure monitoring in a capable adult.

bank.question: A competent patient refuses a routine blood test because they have a phobia of needles. What is the most appropriate next step?
bank.explanation: In a non-emergency, the patient's right to refuse treatment must be respected. You should explore their reasons to ensure they are informed.
options: Tell the patient they must have the blood test or they will not be allowed to stay in hospital.
Ask the nursing staff to hold the patient's arm still so you can quickly take the sample.
Document that the patient is being 'difficult' and try again later without talking to them.
Respect the refusal, explore their reasons, and explain the importance of the test.

bank.question: You see a colleague has posted a photo of a patient's unusual skin rash on a public social media group, asking for diagnostic advice. What should you do?
bank.explanation: Social media use must maintain professional boundaries and patient confidentiality; discussing specific cases online is a breach of GMC guidance.
options: Comment on the post with your clinical opinion to help the patient.
'Like' the post to show support for your colleague's hard work.
Advise your colleague privately to remove the post immediately.
Report the colleague to the GMC as your first course of action.

bank.question: A consultant asks you to prescribe a dose of a medication that you believe is significantly higher than the recommended safety limit. What is the most appropriate action?
bank.explanation: Patient safety is paramount; if the dose is dangerously high/unsafe, you must not prescribe it and should discuss your concerns with the senior doctor.
options: Prescribe the dose as requested as the consultant is more experienced.
Ask a nurse if they think the dose is appropriate before prescribing.
Politely explain your concerns to the consultant and decline to prescribe it if you believe it is unsafe.
Prescribe the dose but write a note in the records that you disagree with the decision.

bank.question: A doctor's professional conduct and the standards set by the General Medical Council (GMC) apply to their behavior both inside and outside of the workplace.
bank.explanation: The GMC 'Good Medical Practice' guidance applies to a doctor's conduct at all times, including their private and social media activity.

bank.question: While you are performing a routine venepuncture, the patient suddenly says, 'I changed my mind, I don't want this anymore.' How should you respond?
bank.explanation: You must stop and listen to the patient's concerns; proceed only if they give informed consent after you have addressed their worries.
options: Stop the procedure immediately and ask the patient why they are concerned.
Continue the procedure quickly to get it over with so the patient feels better.
Tell the patient that the procedure is necessary and they must stay still.
Ask a nurse to hold the patient's arm steady so you can finish the blood draw.

bank.question: You realise you prescribed the wrong 'once-daily' medication for a patient. The dose was given, but the patient is stable and unharmed. What is the best action?
bank.explanation: The duty of candour requires doctors to be honest with patients when something goes wrong, regardless of whether harm occurred.
options: Say nothing as the patient was not harmed and it might cause unnecessary anxiety.
Explain the error to the patient, apologise, and monitor them for side effects.
Ask the nurse who administered the drug to explain the mistake to the patient.
Wait for the consultant to decide whether the patient should be told.

bank.question: When is the most appropriate time to document a clinical review you have performed on a patient?
bank.explanation: Clinical notes should be completed as soon as possible after the event to ensure accuracy and continuity of care.
options: At the very end of your shift when all tasks are complete.
As soon as possible after the review or procedure has taken place.
The following morning before the consultant ward round begins.
Once a week during a dedicated administration session.

bank.question: If you suspect a senior consultant is frequently coming to work under the influence of alcohol, you should ignore it to avoid damaging their career and your own progression.
bank.explanation: Doctors have a duty to act if they believe a colleague's health or performance poses a risk to patients, even if they are a senior member of staff.

bank.question: You are preparing to discharge a patient with mild dementia. What is the most important step to ensure they manage their medications safely at home?
bank.explanation: Involving the family/carers is vital for patient safety and successful recovery when the patient has specific needs like dementia.
options: Assume the patient understands everything and provide written leaflets only.
With the patient's permission, involve their family or carers in the discharge discussion.
Delay the discharge indefinitely until the patient's memory improves.
Ask the ward clerk to explain the medications to the patient.

bank.question: While assisting a consultant with a sterile procedure, you notice they accidentally touch a non-sterile curtain with their glove. What should you do?
bank.explanation: Maintaining the sterile field and patient safety is more important than hierarchy; any breach in asepsis must be addressed immediately.
options: Point out the break in technique immediately and offer a new pair of sterile gloves.
Say nothing to avoid embarrassing a senior colleague in front of the patient.
Wait until the procedure is finished to mention it privately.
Document the breach in the patient's notes after the procedure is over.

bank.question: You realise you accidentally omitted a dose of a patient's regular antibiotic. What is your first responsibility regarding the patient?
bank.explanation: Under the Duty of Candour, you must inform the patient of mistakes, apologise, and explain the steps being taken.
options: Monitor the patient closely and only tell them if they develop side effects.
Do nothing, as one missed dose of an antibiotic is unlikely to cause harm.
Ask the pharmacist to speak to the patient on your behalf.
Inform the patient of the error, apologise, and document the conversation in the notes.

bank.question: A patient has a legal right to view their own medical records, although the hospital may charge a reasonable administrative fee for making any paper copies.
bank.explanation: Patients have a legal right to access their own medical records under the Data Protection Act 2018 and GDPR, though some exceptions apply regarding third-party data.

bank.question: You are handing over to the night team. What is the most effective way to ensure a safe transition of care?
bank.explanation: Patient handover is a critical point for safety; it must be structured (e.g., SBAR) and prioritise the most unwell patients.
options: Give a brief summary of every patient in alphabetical order.
Hand over only the patients who are expected to be discharged the next day.
Use a structured format (like SBAR) to highlight the most unwell patients and outstanding tasks.
Leave a pile of printed notes on the desk for the night team to read.

bank.question: A patient with advanced dementia and no family requires an urgent but non-life-threatening treatment. They cannot understand the information. What is the next step?
